newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac wants closer ties with Japan after N-tests.
newsitem.headline: Chirac wants closer ties with Japan after N-tests.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, a lover of Japanese art, visits Tokyo from Sunday to bolster trade and seal a recovery of ties bruised last year by Paris' nuclear tests in the South Pacific.

A student of Japanese culture who made more than 40 trips to Japan before becoming president last year, Chirac will visit from November 17-22 hoping to step up economic links with a nation that looks more to the United States for partnership than to Europe.

"There are margins for progress," Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said of economic ties. "Japan should continue to open itself," she said, pointing to areas such as food, aerospace and insurance.
She added that France did not consider Tokyo protectionist.
Chirac, who twinned Tokyo with Paris when he was mayor of the French capital, is to meet Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and announce a 20-point action accord between the two nations.

France's 1995 trade deficit with Japan was 20 billion francs ($3.9 billion) with exports of 28 billion ($5.5 billion) and imports of 47.5 billion (9.3 billion). The nuclear tests, which ended in January, led to calls in Japan to boycott French goods.
Chirac wants to triple France's share of Japan's imports from a current two percent within a decade.

With the end of the Cold War "the world is no longer bi-polar," Colonna told reporters. "We must organise the Europe-Asia link which is the weak side of the triangle between the United States, Europe and Japan."

Chirac outraged many Japanese with six nuclear tests from September 1995, a month after the 50th anniversary of the devastating World War Two nuclear bombings of the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Anti-nuclear protestors plan to demonstrate outside the French embassy in Tokyo on Sunday and urge Chirac to visit Hiroshima and Nagasaki rather than Fukuoka, where he plans to visit a sumo wrestling tournament before flying home on Friday.
"The nuclear problem is not over yet," said Icihiro Murakami, a leading member of a Tokyo anti-nuclear group, saying it was a first opportunity for Japanese to confront Chirac.
But Japanese and French officials say France's six final atomic tests are no longer an issue after the two countries agreed in May to put the dispute behind them.

Chirac has already put off the trip. In September 1995, he said he had no plans to take up an invitation to visit Japan after a Japanese cabinet minister took part in an anti-nuclear demonstration in French Polynesia.
Chirac will be accompanied by Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy and Telecommunications and Space Minister Francois Fillon.
Bosses from companies such as pharmaceuticals maker Sanofi and aircraft and space firm Aerospatiale will also travel with Chirac.
Chirac will also seek to bolster cultural ties. France is to stage a year of exhibitions about Japan in 1997 and Japan will reciprocate in 1998.
